summary: Defines additional RADIUS attributes for IEEE 802 networks and clarifies how the EAP-Key-Name and Called-Station-Id attributes are used. It updates RFC 3580 and RFC 4072.

eli5.summary: When you join a Wi-Fi or wired network, a central check decides if you may enter. This adds more fields to the messages for that check.

subtitle: New RADIUS attributes that let Wi-Fi and wired 802 access points tell a central server more and get more back.

tldr.problem: Access points and switches that use RADIUS for central authentication, authorization and accounting in IEEE 802 networks needed more attributes than RFC 3580 provided, and the use of EAP-Key-Name and Called-Station-Id needed clarifying.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines 17 new RADIUS attributes (types 174 to 190), such as Allowed-Called-Station-Id, Network-Id-Name and the WLAN-* family, and sets rules for how EAP-Key-Name is sent and checked.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 3580 and RFC 4072, and it is itself updated by RFC 8044.

today: RFC 7268 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 3580 and RFC 4072. It is itself updated by RFC 8044 and has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why IEEE 802 Needs More RADIUS Attributes
sections.content:
Where authentication, authorization and accounting (AAA) for IEEE 802 networks is managed centrally, a backend server is used and the IEEE 802 authenticators act as AAA clients. RFC 3580 gave guidelines for using RADIUS in such networks. RFC 7268 defines additional attributes suited to authenticators acting as AAA clients, and it clarifies the use of the EAP-Key-Name and Called-Station-Id attributes.

Each attribute section follows the same pattern: a description of where the attribute may appear, a Type number, a Length and a Value or String field. The RFC borrows many value definitions directly from IEEE 802.11 and IEEE 802.1X rather than inventing new ones.

The terms used are Access Point, Association, Authenticator, Authentication Server, Station and Supplicant. The key words MUST, SHOULD and MAY carry their RFC 2119 meanings.
sections.eli5: A big building has one front desk that checks everybody's badge. This RFC gives the doors extra things they can tell the desk, like which door you are at and what kind of room it is.

sections.title: Naming the Network and the Access Point
sections.content:
Allowed-Called-Station-Id (type 174) lets the RADIUS server tell the authenticator which MAC addresses and/or networks a user may connect to. It may appear in an Access-Accept, CoA-Request or Accounting-Request. It is useful with pre-authentication, where the Access-Request usually has no Called-Station-Id and the server does not know which network the user is trying to reach. If the Called-Station-Id the user connects to matches none of these attributes, the Network Access Server MUST NOT permit access.

For IEEE 802, the value is a MAC address as uppercase ASCII with octets separated by a dash character, for example 00-10-A4-23-19-C0. To restrict both MAC address and network, append the network name after a :, as in 00-10-A4-23-19-C0:AP1. To restrict only the network, omit the MAC address but keep the colon, as in :AP1.

Network-Id-Name (type 179) carries the IEEE 802.1X Network-Id name (NID-Name). An 802.11 SSID is at most 32 octets, but a NID-Name can be up to 253 octets, which may not fit beside a MAC address. So with 802.1X the Called-Station-Id SHOULD hold only the MAC address and Network-Id-Name carries the NID-Name. Network-Id-Name MUST NOT be used for an 802.11 SSID.

WLAN-HESSID (type 181) carries the MAC address of the Homogenous Extended Service Set, which together with the SSID can identify a subscription service provider network. Its length is 19 and it uses the same dash-separated format.
sections.eli5: These fields say which door and which building you are using. Because some building names are very long, the door number and the building name travel in separate boxes.

sections.title: EAP Names and Key Names
sections.content:
Three attributes carry names produced by EAP. EAP-Key-Name (type 102, defined in RFC 4072) holds the EAP Session-Id described in RFC 5247. EAP-Peer-Id (type 175) and EAP-Server-Id (type 176) hold a Peer-Id and a Server-Id exported by the EAP method.

The NAS is a pass-through in EAP, so it cannot know these values before the RADIUS server tells it. The RFC therefore requires that in an Access-Request each of these attributes MUST contain only a single NUL character. A server that receives anything else MUST silently discard the attribute. The server SHOULD include the attribute in an Access-Accept only if the Access-Request carried it.

For EAP-Key-Name there is a stricter consequence. A NAS normally asks for it only when it needs it to provision service. If it was in the Access-Request but is missing from the Access-Accept, the NAS SHOULD treat the Access-Accept as an Access-Reject. If it was not requested but arrives anyway, the NAS SHOULD silently discard it.

The reason is MACsec. The Connectivity Association Key Name (CKN) is derived from the EAP Session-Id and is later used to derive the keys that protect the Secure Association Keys. To take part in the MACsec Key Agreement exchange, the NAS needs EAP-Key-Name from the server.
sections.eli5: The door guard cannot know a secret code word until the front desk says it, so the guard sends a blank card first. The desk fills it in, and if it comes back blank when the guard needed it, the guard says no.

sections.title: Session and Reason Attributes
sections.content:
Mobility-Domain-Id (type 177, length 6) lets the NAS give the server the IEEE 802.11 Mobility Domain Identifier in an Access-Request or Accounting-Request. The value is a 32-bit integer: the two most significant octets MUST be zero when sent, and the two least significant carry the identifier.

Preauth-Timeout (type 178, length 6) sets the maximum number of seconds the NAS must keep pre-authentication state that has not been used in a user session. With 802.11 pre-authentication, a Pairwise Master Key not used within that time MAY be discarded by the access point. It has no bearing on the session time once the session is underway, which the Session-Timeout attribute determines.

EAPoL-Announcement (type 180) carries IEEE 802.1X EAPoL-Announcement TLVs between the NAS and the server. Several attributes in one packet have their strings concatenated before parsing, and a TLV longer than 253 octets MUST be fragmented across attributes.

WLAN-Reason-Code (type 185, length 6) says why a Station was refused access. It MAY appear in an Access-Reject, Disconnect-Request or Accounting-Request. When the access point receives it in an Access-Reject or Disconnect-Request, the value is copied into the Reason Code field of the Disassociation or Deauthentication frame sent to the Station.
sections.eli5: These are small notes passed along the way. One says how long to keep a visitor pass warm, and one tells the guard what reason to give someone who is turned away.

sections.title: Describing the Wireless Link and Venue
sections.content:
Several attributes let an access point describe the wireless situation to the server in an Access-Request or Accounting-Request.

  • WLAN-Venue-Info (182): a Venue Group octet (for example Assembly) and a Venue Type octet (for example Library), with codes defined by IEEE 802.11.
  • WLAN-Venue-Language (183) and WLAN-Venue-Name (184): the language of the name that follows, and the venue name itself in UTF-8, up to 252 octets. Several names in different languages may be sent.
  • WLAN-Pairwise-Cipher (186), WLAN-Group-Cipher (187), WLAN-AKM-Suite (188) and WLAN-Group-Mgmt-Cipher (189): the ciphersuites and authentication and key management suite used to set up the robust security network association between the access point and the device, each as a 32-bit suite selector.
  • WLAN-RF-Band (190): the radio frequency band used by the access point.

The presence of WLAN-Group-Mgmt-Cipher indicates that the Station negotiated management frame protection during association.
sections.eli5: The access point can tell the front desk what kind of place it is in, what language its sign uses, what lock type the connection uses, and which radio channel family it is on.

sections.title: Attribute Numbers and the Packet Table
sections.content:
The RFC takes new attribute types from the existing RADIUS namespace of RFC 2865. Types 174 to 190 are assigned to the 17 new attributes. Because the values come from IEEE 802, no new registries are created for IANA to maintain.

Section 3 gives a table showing which attributes may appear in which packet types, and how many times. The codes are 0 (MUST NOT be present), 0+ (zero or more) and 0-1 (zero or one). For example, WLAN-Reason-Code is allowed only in Access-Reject, Disconnect-Request and Accounting-Request, while EAPoL-Announcement may appear in all packet types listed.
sections.eli5: Each new field gets its own number so everybody can find it, like giving every locker in a school a number.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Using RADIUS for AAA in IEEE 802 networks inherits all the threats of other RADIUS uses, discussed in RFC 2607, RFC 2865, RFC 3162, RFC 3579, RFC 3580 and RFC 5176. If RADIUS traffic is sent in the clear, an attacker snooping the exchange can read the attributes defined here, so RADIUS confidentiality is desirable (see RFC 6421).

A server could accept or reject an Access-Request based on the cipher, AKM or RF band attributes, but the RFC says the value of doing so is limited. Rejections should normally be unnecessary except where access points and Stations are misconfigured, and fixing the misconfiguration serves users better. Where access must be rejected, the user should be told why. For unacceptable cipher or AKM values, a WLAN-Reason-Code of 29 SHOULD be returned in the Access-Reject. For an unacceptable WLAN-RF-Band, the code is 11.
sections.eli5: Notes sent in the open can be read by snoopers, so they should be kept in a sealed envelope. And if someone is turned away, they should be told why.
